stats-simpson-s1.title: Two meadows with the same five species
stats-simpson-s1.text: Ecologists counted the flowering plants in 1 m² quadrats in two meadows. Both meadows contain the same five species.

table.caption: Number of plants of each species

stats-simpson-s2.title: A stream bank before and after a fast-spreading plant arrived
stats-simpson-s2.text: A survey of 100 plants along a stream bank was repeated eight years after a fast-growing plant from another continent (species X) began spreading there.

table.caption: Number of plants of each species

items.q: Calculate Simpson's diversity index for meadow A, to two decimal places.

why.correct: Each species is 20/100 = 0.2 of the total. (0.2)² = 0.04, and five species give Σ = 0.20. D = 1 − 0.20 = 0.80.

items.q: Calculate Simpson's diversity index for meadow B, to two decimal places.
Both meadows have five species. Why is meadow B's index so much lower?
options: Meadow B is dominated by clover, so its species are unevenly represented, and the index counts evenness as well as the number of species.
Meadow B has fewer individual plants in total, and Simpson's index falls whenever the total number of plants counted in the quadrats is smaller.
Meadow B has fewer species than meadow A, because four of its species have just five plants each.
Meadow B's clover plants are larger than meadow A's, and the index weighs each species by the size of its plants.

why.correct: Richness (5) is the same. In B one species makes up 80% of plants, so two plants picked at random are very likely the same species, which is what a low D means.
options: Correct: same richness, very different evenness.
Both totals are 100.
Both meadows have five species; rare species still count toward richness.
The index uses counts of individuals, not their size.

items.q: A disease kills most of the clover in both meadows. Which prediction is best supported?
options: Meadow B loses far more of its plants, because clover made up most of them; meadow A's plants are spread among species.
Both meadows lose the same share of their plants, because clover is one of five species in each meadow.
Meadow A loses more plant cover, because a more diverse meadow has more species for the disease to infect.
Neither meadow changes much, because the other four species immediately take over the space that the dying clover plants leave behind.

why.correct: Clover is 80% of B's plants but 20% of A's. Losing it removes most of B's plants but only a fifth of A's: more even communities tend to keep functioning when one species declines.
options: Correct.
The share differs: 80% in B, 20% in A.
The disease attacks clover here, not every species.
Regrowth takes time, and B has very few plants of the other species to fill the gap.

items.q: Calculate Simpson's index for the first survey, to three decimal places.
Calculate Simpson's index eight years later, to three decimal places.
Calculate the percent change in Simpson's index between the surveys, to the nearest whole percent (use a minus sign for a decrease).
Species richness was 5 in both surveys. Which statement best describes how the community changed?
options: Richness stayed at 5 because species X replaced violet, but evenness fell sharply as X came to make up 70% of the plants.
Diversity did not change, because the number of species was the same in both surveys and richness is what diversity measures.
Diversity rose, because a new species arrived, and adding a species to a community raises its diversity index.
Each native species increased in number, but species X increased faster, which lowered the index.

why.correct: One species was lost and one gained, so richness is unchanged. The fall in D comes from dominance: X is 70% of plants, so evenness collapsed.
options: Correct.
Simpson's index measures evenness as well as richness; it fell from 0.775 to 0.484.
X's arrival came with violet's loss and with heavy dominance, so D fell.
Every native species decreased (sedge 30 to 12, and so on).

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the change in the native species' numbers?
options: Species X competed with the native plants for light, water and space, and its fast growth let it take most of these limited resources.
Species X produced food that the native plants needed, so the natives became dependent on it and stopped growing.
The native plants evolved to become less numerous, so that species X would have room to grow on the bank.
The native plants moved upstream to avoid species X, so they were no longer within the area of the survey.

why.correct: Plants on a stream bank compete for limited light, water, nutrients and space. A fast-spreading competitor can take most of them, reducing native numbers (interspecific competition).
options: Correct.
Plants make their own food; nothing suggests dependence on X.
Populations do not shrink "so that" another species can grow; that is a purpose, not a mechanism.
Rooted plants do not move away; their numbers changed through survival and reproduction.

items.q: What does a Simpson's index of 0 mean?
options: The community contains a single species.
The quadrats held no organisms to count.
The community is perfectly even across many species.
The community has exactly two species in equal numbers.

why.correct: With one species, n/N = 1, so Σ = 1 and D = 1 − 1 = 0: two individuals picked at random are certainly the same species.
options: Correct.
With no organisms the index cannot be calculated (N = 0).
Many even species give D close to 1.
Two equal species give D = 1 − (0.25 + 0.25) = 0.5.

items.q: A pond sample has 6 snails, 3 beetles and 1 leech. Calculate Simpson's index, to two decimal places.
One plant of a sixth species is found in meadow A (which had 20 each of five species, D = 0.80). What happens to Simpson's index?
options: It rises only slightly, to about 0.80, because a species with one individual adds almost nothing to the sum of squares.
It rises to about 0.83, because adding a species raises the index by roughly one sixth of its old value.
It falls, because the new species has far fewer plants than the others and makes the community less even.
It does not change, because Simpson's index ignores species that make up less than 1% of the community.

why.correct: N = 101. Σ = 5 × (20/101)² + (1/101)² = 0.1960 + 0.0001 = 0.1961. D = 0.804. Rare species barely move Simpson's index, which is dominated by common ones.
options: Correct: from 0.800 to 0.804.
The rise is tiny, not a sixth.
A rare new species still slightly lowers Σ(n/N)², so D rises a little.
It is included; its effect is just very small.

items.q: A student reports a Simpson's index of 0.65 for meadow B. What mistake did the student most likely make?
options: Reporting Σ(n/N)² without subtracting it from 1
Using percentages instead of fractions for each species
Leaving the rare species out of the calculation
Squaring the total number of plants instead of each fraction

why.correct: For meadow B, Σ(n/N)² = 0.65, so D = 1 − 0.65 = 0.35. Forgetting the "1 −" reports the chance two random plants are the same species instead of different.
options: Correct.
Percentages would give numbers in the thousands, not 0.65.
Leaving out the rare species gives Σ = 0.64 and D = 0.36, not 0.65.
That would not produce 0.65.

items.q: Put the steps for calculating Simpson's diversity index in order.
options: Count the individuals of each species (n) and the total (N).
Divide each n by N.
Square each fraction.
Add the squares.
Subtract the sum from 1.

why.correct: D = 1 − Σ(n/N)²: count, divide, square, add, subtract from 1.

items.q: Two forests have Simpson's indices of 0.91 and 0.62. Which claim is justified?
options: The forest with 0.91 is more diverse: two trees picked at random are more likely to be different species.
The forest with 0.91 has more species, because Simpson's index measures the number of species present.
The forest with 0.62 is more diverse, because a lower index means that species are spread out more evenly.
The forest with 0.91 has more trees in total, because the index rises with the number of individuals counted.

why.correct: Higher D means higher diversity: richness and evenness together. D is the probability that two individuals picked at random belong to different species.
options: Correct.
D combines richness and evenness; a higher D does not by itself mean more species.
A higher D, not a lower one, means more even and diverse.
D depends on proportions, not on the total count.
